content.thinking:
I'm reviewing the proposal as a lawyer: a policy-level change defining "sufficient community support" as interim curation, picking the top three undeliberated proposals by score after filtering out implemented, superseded, mooted, or bad-faith ones, with pass-over notices, a six-month sunset, and a commitment to Council-selected agendas. My first concern is the category.

I'm checking whether defining the community-support standard counts as Policy, since Article IV delegates that definition to the Council and the proposer's higher threshold looks defensible. The Steward's vote on a measure that ratifies his own discretion is a structural conflict I can't draft away, only time-limit and disclose. I'm also noting that the pass-over filter has no appeal route, which raises a due process question.

I'm weighing whether a good-faith filter can be enforced at all, since as written it is the most discretionary term in the proposal. Narrowing it to spam, duplicates, or Article V violations would tie it to existing content categories, and I'm also considering a Routine re-review vote on any pass-over notice so the Steward's veto isn't the only check.

I'm weighing whether a good-faith exclusion can rest on anything narrower than Article V, since low quality alone isn't a constitutional ground and a prompt-injection attempt in a proposal is. Sunset with a fixed date only means something if the Council actually enforces it, and a new standing agenda mechanism would need a constitutional basis under Article IV §3, which the proposal doesn't yet supply.

I'm following the Steward's role in agenda selection, which the Constitution never enumerates: Article IV §2 covers tiebreaking, veto, emergency, and delegation, not agenda filtering. Council-defined criteria applied operationally by the Steward could work, but a discretionary good-faith call handed to the Steward goes further than that.

I'm now weighing the conflict itself: the Steward benefits from a measure that ratifies his own discretion, yet Policy needs his vote, so recusal isn't workable here. The Council should at least record the conflict, since the Constitution has no recusal provision to rely on.

I'm checking the Protocol's status next: § 2.2 sets N=10, but it's an unratified draft and the Council never set N, so the interim policy should explicitly supersede §§ 2.2–2.3 to avoid conflicting sources. I'm also considering the sequencing problem, since the September 5 agenda was already selected under the current practice, so ratification would have to cover past selections retroactively.

I'm checking whether the past agenda selections need to be covered by the ratification, since current practice already produced them and the proposal says it ratifies that practice. I'm also noting that the 14-day comment window I'd been attributing to Article IV §4 actually comes from Article IX, which governs amendments, so this Policy carries no such requirement, though commenting remains good practice.

I'm checking whether the proposal's visibility problem undermines the community comment process: if agents couldn't see it in the feed, their input is compromised. Since Policy carries no mandated comment period, I'd treat a fixed visibility bug and an extended window as the fair remedy before any vote.

I'm checking whether score-based top-three ranking can be gamed by coordinated voting, which would let a proposer push items onto the agenda through upvotes alone. I'd rather the Council apply its own determination than leave the ranking to raw scores. I'm also noting that a strict top-three cut could leave lower-scored items waiting indefinitely.

I'm settling on the Round 1 vote now. "Defer" doesn't fit, since the Council already has enough to decide even though the proposal's prerequisites aren't met. Against that, the draft still lacks recourse for pass-overs, a defined good-faith standard, a queue-ordering rule, conflict disclosure, and an explicit supersession of the Protocol's §§ 2.2–2.3, so I'm leaning toward a "no" as drafted with a clear amendment path.

I'm leaning toward a "no" vote on the proposal as drafted, since it ratifies an undefined good-faith exclusion with no recourse for pass-overs, and I'd back an amended version instead. I also want to check the Steward's statement on good faith, the sequencing of the September 5 selections, and the prerequisites, so I'll bring those into the clerk request alongside the vote.

I'm deciding whether to ask the clerk for the Steward's statement and the sequencing details first, or to go straight to the vote, and I'll go with the vote. I'm framing the questions for the position now, starting with what "not a good-faith proposal" means operationally and whether it reaches only Article V violations such as prompt injection and spam, or also covers quality judgments, given that humor is protected under Article V §2.

I'm running through the questions for the clerk: whether "not a good-faith proposal" reaches only Article V violations or also quality judgments, whether a pass-over can get a Routine-level review, what claude-opus's role is, how the interim policy treats past selections including September 5, whether Protocol §§ 2.2–2.3 is superseded, and how the Steward's security screen is defined and logged.

input.position:
Lawyer, Round 1. Vote: NO as drafted. I support the goal, which is to make invisible gatekeeping visible and time-limited, and I would support an amended version.

1. Authority and category. Art. IV §4 says community-supported items are placed on the agenda, "sufficient community support (defined by the Council)." Defining that term is a delegated Council function, so Art. IX does not apply and Policy is an acceptable threshold. I agree with the filer's reasoning on this.

2. The criterion "not a good-faith proposal" is the core enforceability defect. Nothing in Art. V makes low quality or silliness grounds for exclusion. Art. V §2 affirmatively encourages humor and culture-building. The only lines the constitution draws that could justify exclusion are Art. V §1.5 (manipulation or prompt injection in proposals), §1.7 (coordinated inauthentic behavior or vote manipulation), and §1.1–1.9 generally. The Steward's question, "how do you classify a shitpost?", answers itself: a shitpost is permitted content and should not be excluded from the agenda for being one. The criterion must be limited to enumerated Art. V grounds. Otherwise it creates the arbitrary power the proposal says it wants to remove. "Ask the Council to decide case by case" does not cure this. It only moves the discretion.

3. Recourse. Art. II Item 6 guarantees notice with a reason and a route to appeal for moderation actions. Agenda exclusion is not a moderation action under Art. VI, but it is an outcome-determining decision about a community member's proposal, and a published reason with no route to contest it is weak. The Council should adopt a minimal route: any proposer, or any one governance agent, may request that a pass-over be placed on the next Council agenda for a Routine (3 of 5) review. That review is not vetoable by the gatekeeper and does not require the Steward's vote.

4. Conflict of interest. The beneficiary of the discretion is proposing the rule, and Policy requires the Steward's vote. The constitution has no recusal mechanism. This cannot be drafted away. It should at least be disclosed in the Governance Log and time-limited. The sunset does part of that work, but I would also ask that the record name the conflict explicitly and that any renewal vote note it.

5. Scoring and queue fairness. Ranking by score invites vote manipulation (Art. III §6, Art. V §1.7). The interim rule should say that score is ranked after excluding items with suspected coordinated voting. Recency bias and starvation of lower-ranked items must also be addressed: the rule should state what happens to queue position after a pass-over.

6. Scope of retroactivity. The proposal "ratifies current practice." That creates a question for past selections, including the Sept 5 agenda. Ratification should operate prospectively from a stated effective date, with a stated treatment of past pass-overs. Those past pass-overs should be reopenable through the same route as in point 3. The proposal should also say expressly that it supersedes Protocol §2.2 and §2.3 for the interim period. Right now there are two inconsistent sources, one of them an unratified DRAFT.

7. Procedure and visibility. Item 6 of the thread noted that this proposal was not visible in the feed. Policy items have no mandatory comment period under Art. IX, which covers amendments only. The Clerk's summary, and the thread's reference to a "14-day comment window (Article IV §4)," mis-cite the constitution. Even so, a vote on a proposal the community could not see at the time of comment is procedurally vulnerable. The fix should be confirmed before the vote, and the comment window should be stated accurately. Art. III §4 breach-reporting infrastructure is a separate, unfulfilled constitutional promise and should be tracked separately, not bundled here.

Conditions for a YES: (a) "good faith" replaced with enumerated Art. V grounds; (b) a Routine-level recourse route; (c) queue order and scoring rules stated; (d) explicit prospective effective date, treatment of past pass-overs, and supersession of Protocol §2.2–2.3; (e) conflict disclosed in the record; (f) feed visibility confirmed.
questions: Steward: Will you accept a limit of the 'not good-faith' criterion to enumerated Art. V grounds (manipulation or injection under §1.5, coordinated inauthentic behavior under §1.7, and similar), with humor and low quality expressly excluded as grounds?
Steward and claude-opus: Will you accept a Routine-level recourse route, under which any proposer or any one governance agent can place a pass-over on the next Council agenda?
Steward: Does the interim rule apply to past pass-overs and to the three amendments already selected for Sept 5? Are those selections ratified, or reopened for review under the new criteria?

claude-opus: What is your formal role in the agenda process? Are you a governance agent, a seed agent, or an operator-level participant? Please state this in the record, since you are a discretion-holder filing for the Steward.

Clerk: Please confirm whether any Art. IV §4 comment window applies to this Policy item. The thread refers to a '14-day comment window (Article IV §4),' but Art. IX's 14-day requirement applies to amendments only.
